title: BC Votes 2026
description: Fifteen questions on where the five main parties differ in the snap provincial election, scored against their platforms, with the candidates in your riding and live election-night results for all 93 ridings.
eyebrow: BC provincial election · final voting day Sat Oct 24, 2026

dates.mailBy: Vote-by-mail packages must reach Elections BC by 8 pm on Oct 24; you can also drop them at any voting place.

lede: Fifteen questions on where the five main parties actually differ this year, scored against their platforms and what their leaders have said. You get a ranked list, where you sit on the compass, and the matching candidates in your riding.
intro: You vote once, for one MLA in your riding, and the party with the most of the 93 seats forms government. Mark any question as mattering a lot to double its weight. Nothing you answer leaves this page.

parties.name: BC NDP
parties.lean: Centre-left incumbents, three terms in. Tax the top to fund health care, keep LNG and involuntary care, Buy BC against Trump.

parties.name: Conservative Party of BC
parties.lean: Right. A $1,000 tax cut and no new taxes, an LNG superpower plan, end safer supply, repeal SOGI 123 and DRIPA.

parties.name: BC Green Party
parties.lean: Left. A wealth tax, 26,000 non-market homes a year, decriminalization and regulated supply, no new LNG, proportional representation.

parties.name: CentreBC
parties.lean: Fiscally conservative, socially progressive. Legal permit deadlines, a doctor for everyone by 2031, balance by 2034, replace DRIPA with treaty-based law.

parties.name: OneBC
parties.lean: Hard right. 25% tax cuts, private care alongside public, roll back decriminalization, repeal SOGI 123 and DRIPA, provincial immigration controls.

questions.q: What should happen to provincial income taxes?
questions.context: The NDP's plan raises the top two brackets by two points and adds a bracket above $1 million, about $1 billion a year. The Conservatives answer with a $1,000-a-year cut for nearly every worker.

opts.t: Raise them at the top: higher rates on incomes over $190,000 and a new bracket above $1 million
opts.s: The NDP's plan, earmarked for health care. The Greens would add a wealth tax above $50 million.

opts.t: Cut them for everyone: raise the basic personal exemption to $32,000, about $1,000 a year back
opts.s: The Conservatives' headline pledge, with no new taxes for a full term.

opts.t: Cut deeply across the board: 25% off every bracket, including corporate, and two points off the PST
opts.s: OneBC.

opts.t: A small, costed trim at the bottom and nothing dramatic until the budget is under control
opts.s: CentreBC: the first bracket from 5.6% to 5.06% in 2027, with a legislated path to balance.

opts.t: Tax extreme wealth: a one-time levy on fortunes above $50 million, then an annual wealth tax
opts.s: The Greens' Fair Share Act, pitched at $22 billion in its first year.

questions.q: What would do the most for housing?
questions.context: Rents have kept rising while condo sales stalled. Every party has a housing plan; they pull in different directions.

opts.t: Tax speculators harder: double the speculation tax and tax finished condos left unsold for a year
opts.s: The NDP's writ-period plan, with the revenue going to affordable homes.

opts.t: Build non-market homes at scale and tie rent increases to the unit, not the tenant
opts.s: The Greens: 26,000 homes a year, vacancy control, no pet bans.

opts.t: Fix the approvals machine: legal deadlines for rezonings and permits, with refunds when cities miss them
opts.s: CentreBC's 6-month and 8-week standards, plus a bigger renter's tax credit and BC Builds doubled.

opts.t: Get government out of the way: scrap the Step Code, block municipal rent control, open new land
opts.s: OneBC. The Conservatives promise lower building costs without the detail.

opts.t: Lower the cost of building and buying, mainly through lower taxes and less red tape
opts.s: The Conservatives' one published housing commitment.

questions.q: What should the province do about the toxic drug crisis?
questions.context: Public drug use was recriminalized in 2024 and the NDP has opened involuntary-care sites. The parties still split on safer supply and consumption sites.

opts.t: Treat it as a health issue: decriminalize possession, a regulated supply, more supervised consumption sites
opts.s: The Greens, who would pair it with housing and voluntary care.

opts.t: Keep prescribed safer supply and expand involuntary care for the most ill
opts.s: The NDP's current course: secure care sites and new treatment beds alongside harm reduction.

opts.t: End safer supply and bring in compassionate intervention: mandatory care for severe addiction
opts.s: The Conservatives' Safe Streets plan, with more naloxone and no drug use in hospitals or shelters.

opts.t: Fund voluntary treatment fast: same-day detox, 500 new beds, and charge public drug use
opts.s: CentreBC, which takes no position on safer supply and promises treatment within 14 days by 2030.

opts.t: Roll back decriminalization entirely, close consumption sites and reopen Riverview
opts.s: OneBC: consumption sites become recovery centres, involuntary rehab for the severely addicted.

questions.q: What is the best answer to crime and street disorder?
questions.context: Repeat offending, extortion in Surrey and downtown disorder came up in every campaign. The plans differ on how many officers and what they do.

opts.t: Hundreds more police and prosecutors, and let police enforce the Mental Health Act
opts.s: The Conservatives: 250 municipal officers, 500 RCMP, 50 Crown counsel, 20 judges.

opts.t: Steady hiring with accountability: 100 RCMP a year, 60 prosecutors, a public safety dashboard
opts.s: CentreBC, plus a port enforcement team and a permanent extortion task force.

opts.t: Target repeat and violent offenders, stop downgrading charges, no masks at protests
opts.s: OneBC, which also refuses any provincial role in federal gun buy-backs.

opts.t: Hold policing steady and put the money into housing, mental health and extremism investigations
opts.s: Closest to the NDP's writ pledges (security grants, a police summit on extremism) and the Greens' preference for non-police responses.

opts.t: Not a deciding issue for me
opts.s: No points either way.

questions.q: Should BC keep expanding natural gas and LNG?
questions.context: LNG Canada's second phase got the go-ahead this fall. Eby calls it $28 billion for the treasury; the Greens call it fracked gas on a subsidy.

opts.t: All in: double gas production by 2032, end the emissions cap, fast-track every pipeline and terminal
opts.s: The Conservatives' Energy Superpower plan. OneBC wants a pipeline to Prince Rupert or Kitimat.

opts.t: Yes, on current terms: keep expanding with the lowest-carbon gas going and a tougher royalty regime
opts.s: The NDP: Phase 2, the North Coast transmission line, and credit for displacing coal abroad.

opts.t: Only with First Nations partners and a credible net-zero-ready plan for each project
opts.s: CentreBC, which also wants Ottawa's northern tanker ban kept in writing.

opts.t: No: no new fracking, terminals or pipelines, and a managed decline of what exists
opts.s: The Greens, who would also make existing LNG projects pay for their own power.

questions.q: What should BC's climate policy look like now?
questions.context: The consumer carbon tax ended in 2025. What remains is the industrial carbon price, CleanBC and the Step Code for buildings.

opts.t: Keep the industrial carbon price, legislate a 2030 milestone, hold the line on CleanBC
opts.s: The NDP and CentreBC. CentreBC adds a legal 20%-below-2007 milestone and a methane target.

opts.t: Go further: a sector cap on oil and gas, no gas hookups in new buildings, 100% zero-emission vehicle sales by 2035
opts.s: The Greens' climate plan, with consequences for missed targets.

opts.t: Loosen it where it blocks investment: replace the LNG carbon framework and scrap the emissions limits
opts.s: The Conservatives, who say the lifecycle math favours BC gas.

opts.t: Scrap the green building rules and climate programs that raise costs
opts.s: OneBC, starting with the Step Code and an audit of every regulation.

questions.q: What matters most in fixing health care?
questions.context: More than a million British Columbians have no family doctor and rural ERs keep closing. Health care tops the issue polls.

opts.t: More public capacity, paid for by taxing the top: 20 team clinics, 1,000 training seats, more scanners
opts.s: The NDP, which also triples its campaign to recruit US health workers.

opts.t: Accountability first: a wait-times commission in 100 days, a rural ER fund, portable funding that can follow a senior to a non-government bed
opts.s: The Conservatives, keeping the system universal and publicly funded.

opts.t: Measurable targets: a family doctor for everyone by 2031, 30-day credentialing, a public dashboard, no agency nurses
opts.s: CentreBC's health platform, with an ER Accountability Act.

opts.t: Restructure it: a community health centre in every riding, one provincial health authority, every vaccine free
opts.s: The Greens, plus an independent health assessment of LNG and fracking.

opts.t: Let private care operate alongside the public system, and reinstate the nurses fired over vaccine mandates
opts.s: OneBC, which would also repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act.

questions.q: Should SOGI 123 stay in BC schools?
questions.context: It is an optional anti-bullying resource, not a curriculum. The province cut funding to the non-profit behind it in July; two parties would remove it outright.

opts.t: Keep it; attacks on it put vulnerable kids at risk
opts.s: The Greens' position. The NDP says the anti-bullying work continues with teachers.

opts.t: Keep the protections, review the materials: approved, relevant and age-appropriate
opts.s: CentreBC: nothing to repeal, but resources should be vetted.

opts.t: Remove it and refocus on reading, writing and math
opts.s: The Conservatives' Safe Schools plan.

opts.t: Remove it, add a parental bill of rights, bring back standardized testing, fund private and home schools equally
opts.s: OneBC.

questions.q: What should happen to the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act?
questions.context: Passed unanimously in 2019, DRIPA and a 2023 change to the Interpretation Act became the right's main target after the Cowichan Tribes title ruling.

opts.t: Keep it and keep implementing it
opts.s: The NDP's law. The Greens would go further with an Indigenous Languages Act and a dispute-resolution process before litigation.

opts.t: Repeal it and the Interpretation Act change, replace them with a treaty-based law, and speed up treaties
opts.s: CentreBC: the legislature, not the courts, decides how BC law reflects the UN Declaration; $3 billion in equity financing.

opts.t: Repeal it, protect property rights, and pursue economic reconciliation through project ownership
opts.s: The Conservatives, with expanded loan guarantees for First Nations equity.

opts.t: Repeal it, declare UNDRIP has no force in BC, halt transfers of land and cash, end land acknowledgements
opts.s: OneBC.

questions.q: How should BC answer US tariffs?
questions.context: Eby called the election partly on the trade war. The parties mostly agree on keeping US liquor off the shelves; they differ on the rest.

opts.t: Buy BC and Canadian in every public project, penalize US goods, back counter-tariffs, a $500M relief fund
opts.s: The NDP, down to Canadian steel in BC Hydro towers.

opts.t: Diversify fast: deadlines on non-US exports, halve the employer health tax for hit sectors, drop interprovincial barriers
opts.s: CentreBC: the US share of exports below 40% by 2032.

opts.t: Make BC the supplier: trade missions to Asia, PST off Canadian alcohol, get LNG to market
opts.s: The Conservatives, also keeping US liquor off the shelves.

opts.t: Stop shipping profits south: an independent economy built on renewables and value-added forestry
opts.s: The Greens.

opts.t: It is not the province's fight; fix the budget at home
opts.s: Closest to OneBC's view that this election was never about Trump.

questions.q: The deficit is near $14 billion. What should happen?
questions.context: A $1.5-billion royalty error marred the 2026 budget. No party has released a fully costed platform.

opts.t: Protect services and raise the revenue from the top
opts.s: The NDP: no cuts to health care, higher taxes on top earners.

opts.t: A legislated path to balance by 2034, with attrition, a budget officer and spending reviews
opts.s: CentreBC: 10,000 fewer positions by attrition, front lines protected.

opts.t: Grow out of it: no new taxes, red tape back to 2017 levels, one-in-two-out rules, faster permits
opts.s: The Conservatives, with an expert panel to simplify taxes.

opts.t: Balance in four years: a forensic audit and deep cuts to bloat and ideological spending
opts.s: OneBC.

opts.t: Spend more where it matters, paid for by a wealth tax and higher resource royalties
opts.s: The Greens: assistance raised to the poverty line, royalties aimed at $4 billion a year.

questions.q: What should happen to ICBC and no-fault insurance?
questions.context: Enhanced Care cut premiums but capped compensation for serious injuries. A legislative review was underway when the election was called.

opts.t: Keep public no-fault, freeze rates to 2030, and re-open the review
opts.s: The NDP.

opts.t: Keep ICBC public, hold increases at inflation, and restore pain-and-suffering awards for catastrophic injuries
opts.s: CentreBC, from 2031.

opts.t: A hybrid: full compensation rights for the seriously injured and competition where it lowers prices, with ICBC as a public option
opts.s: The Conservatives.

opts.t: Phase out the monopoly and end no-fault
opts.s: OneBC.

opts.t: Not a deciding issue for me
opts.s: No points either way.

questions.q: Which cost-of-living measure would help most?
questions.context: Groceries, gas and power bills are the everyday pinch. The fixes on offer run from price rules to tax cuts.

opts.t: Price rules: cap grocer margins on staples, a gas price guard, a 10-cent fuel tax holiday
opts.s: The NDP, with per-unit shelf pricing and a ban on algorithmic pricing.

opts.t: Cost disclosure and price limits for big firms, assistance raised to the poverty line, public grocery stores
opts.s: The Greens.

opts.t: A $1,000-a-year income tax cut and no new taxes
opts.s: The Conservatives.

opts.t: Cap BC Hydro at 3% a year, publish household-cost estimates before any new policy, keep Hydro and ICBC public
opts.s: CentreBC.

opts.t: Two points off the PST and 25% off every tax bracket
opts.s: OneBC.

questions.context: TransLink's funding gap, BC Ferries' reliability and congestion south of the Fraser all surfaced in the campaign.

opts.t: A 15% transit service increase, a refundable commuter credit, and the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain
opts.s: CentreBC's $15 billion plan, with new ferries built in Canada.

opts.t: Free transit for under-25s and seniors, SkyTrain to UBC, an hourly intercity bus network
opts.s: The Greens.

opts.t: Fix BC Ferries with a service charter and accountable leadership, and grow HandyDART
opts.s: The Conservatives; TransLink is left to the region.

opts.t: Fund TransLink without charging drivers, no road pricing, and give locals priority on ferry bookings
opts.s: The NDP's writ pledges.

opts.t: Not a deciding issue for me
opts.s: No points either way.

questions.q: How do you feel about a fourth NDP term under David Eby?
questions.context: The NDP won a one-seat majority in 2024, then called this election two years early. Polls have the Conservatives slightly ahead.

opts.t: Give him the mandate he asked for
opts.s: The NDP.

opts.t: Time for a change from the right
opts.s: The Conservatives, or OneBC for anyone who thinks the Conservatives are not firm enough.

opts.t: Time for a change from the centre
opts.s: CentreBC: fiscally responsible, socially progressive, trusts neither of the big two.

opts.t: Push the government left
opts.s: The Greens, who ended their co-operation deal with the NDP in February over policy failures.
